title: AAFP and ISFM Feline Environmental Needs Guidelines
excerpt: The guidelines recommend providing adequate resources in multi-cat households, including separate resting areas that allow cats to see without being seen. Vertical space utilization through cat trees, shelves, and perches at various heights allows cats to establish territories and avoid confrontations. Visual barriers such as screens, furniture arrangements, and partial dividers help reduce stress by allowing cats to control their visual access to other cats while maintaining auditory and olfactory communication.

title: Environmental enrichment strategies for domestic cats: A review of the literature
excerpt: Research indicates that environmental modifications including vertical space (shelves, perches at heights of 90-150cm) and visual barriers significantly reduce aggression and stress in multi-cat households. Partial barriers that allow cats to see around but not directly at each other provide optimal conditions for social buffering while maintaining territorial boundaries. Studies show that cats prefer elevated resting positions and use visual screening to manage social interactions.

title: International Cat Care - How to help cats get along
excerpt: International Cat Care recommends creating separate territories within the home using visual barriers such as bookshelves, screens, or room dividers. These barriers should be high enough (approximately 100-120cm) to block direct line of sight while allowing cats to hear and smell each other. This creates a 'social buffer zone' that reduces tension in multi-cat households by giving cats the option to avoid visual confrontation while remaining aware of each other's presence.
